newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition pots and pans drown state TV.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition pots and pans drown state TV.

text.p: Thousands of opposition supporters beat pots and pans in their apartments in an unusual protest against election fraud which stole their victory in the capital and 14 other towns across Serbia.

Belgrade students called on the citizens to start banging at 5.30 p.m. on Thursday with the aim of -- at least symbolically -- drowning out state television, which they say has ignored or distorted their protests.

Opponents of socialist President Slobodan Milosevic say state television downplays the extent of the protest marches which have thronged the capital and many other towns for 46 days, drawing up to a quarter of a million people.
"I thought the opposition was on the march again, the racket is so loud," Nada, a 74-year-old opposition supporter, said from her apartment in the centre of Belgrade.
The ear-splitting racket lasted for 20 minutes and was heard in most Belgrade districts.
Dedinje, the residential district where Milosevic and other members of the ruling elite have their homes, was one of the few parts of Belgrade that stayed silent.

The opposition accused Belgrade city authorities of deliberately delaying ice-clearing operations after icy rain on Thursday made a dangerous adventure of walking the streets of the capital city fo two million people.

The socialist city authorities, who refused to hand over power to the opposition Zajedno coalition after the November local election in Belgrade and 14 other cities, have not cleared the icy pavements. Hospitals reported scores of limb injuries and fractures during the day.
"They want to make moving in the city as difficult as possible to discourage people attending our rallies," a Zajedno official said.

Milosevic's feared police banned marches through the capital after clashes on December 24 when hardline socialist party (SPS) leaders organised a counter-rally in Belgrade. One person was killed and more than 50 people were injured in street fighting.

Sources close to the SPS acknowledged that one of the main reasons for the ban was fear of growing support for the marchers from citizens who had waved, applauded, cheered and thrown confetti along their route.
About 250,000 Zajedno faithful welcomed the New Year in Belgrade with a city-centre rally featuring ringing alarm clocks as a shrill warning to Milosevic that his "time is up".
State television showed New Year street celebrations in foreign cities but ignored the huge outdoor festival in its own capital.
The influential Serbian Orthodox Church, long a pillar of autocratic government, broke six weeks of silence on Thursday by condemning the SPS for election fraud.
An opposition leader warned that the wave of unrest might turn violent under police pressure and could lead to "bloodshed and civil war".
Vuk Draskovic, a Zajedno leader, claimed in a Reuters Television interview that Milosevic was plotting bloody repression with the help of shadowy militia gangs.

Draskovic said Zajedno's principle of non-violence remained intact but if police attacks worsened, "nobody can give guarantees people would not reply in a way of self-defence to protect their lives and human dignity".

Western governments have told Milosevic that Yugoslavia can forget about reconstruction aid for an economy prostrated by U.N. sanctions and SPS corruption unless he restores Zajedno's election victories and starts broader democratic reform.
